claim: Ticks rely on vertebrate blood as their sole food source throughout their development.
source: Ticks rely on vertebrate blood as their sole food source throughout their development, although it is nutritionally unbalanced.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction section of the manuscript.

claim: Blood contains high levels of proteins, iron, and salts, but low levels of carbohydrates, lipids, and vitamins.
source: Blood contains high levels of proteins, iron, and salts, but low levels of carbohydrates, lipids, and vitamins.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about blood composition.

claim: Tick genomes do not contain genes for synthesis of some essential vitamins.
source: Yet, tick genomes do not contain genes for synthesis of some essential vitamins, thus, vitamin-provisioning pathways have indirectly arisen from symbiotic associations with transovarially transmitted intracellular bacteria (Ben-Yosef et al., 2020; Duron et al., 2018; Duron and Gottlieb, 2020; Gerhart et al., 2016; Gottlieb et al., 2015; Guizzo et al., 2017; Smith et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Most tick species typically harbor a single lineage of nutritional symbiont.
source: Most tick species typically harbor a single lineage of nutritional symbiont, but multiple symbiont lineages exist in different tick species (Duron and Gottlieb, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The most common nutritional symbiont lineages in ticks belong to the Coxiella-like endosymbiont group and to the Francisella-like endosymbiont group.
source: The most common lineages belong to the Coxiella-like endosymbiont group and to the Francisella-like endosymbiont group (CLE and FLE, hereafter) (Azagi et al., 2017; Binetruy et al., 2020; Duron et al., 2017; Machado-Ferreira et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Ticks deprived of their nutritional symbionts show a complete stop of growth and moulting, as well as lethal physical abnormalities.
source: Once deprived of their nutritional symbionts, ticks show a complete stop of growth and moulting, as well as lethal physical abnormalities (Ben-Yosef et al., 2020; Duron et al., 2018; Guizzo et al., 2017; Zhong et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: Lethal physical abnormalities in ticks deprived of nutritional symbionts can be fully restored with an artificial supplement of B vitamins.
source: Once deprived of their nutritional symbionts, ticks show a complete stop of growth and moulting, as well as lethal physical abnormalities (Ben-Yosef et al., 2020; Duron et al., 2018; Guizzo et al., 2017; Zhong et al., 2007), which can be fully restored with an artificial supplement of B vitamins (Duron et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an experimental study.

claim: Nutritional symbionts of ticks have been found primarily in two tick organs, the ovaries and Malpighian tubules.
source: They have been found primarily in two tick organs, the ovaries and Malpighian tubules, while other organs have only been found sporadically infected (Buysse et al., 2019; Duron and Gottlieb, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Genomes of CLE and FLE consistently contain complete biosynthesis pathways of biotin, riboflavin, and folate.
source: Genomes of CLE and FLE consistently contain complete biosynthesis pathways of the same three B vitamins: biotin (vitamin B7), riboflavin (B2), and folate (B9) (Duron et al., 2018; Gerhart et al., 2018; Gerhart et al., 2016; Gottlieb et al., 2015; Guizzo et al., 2017; Nardi et al., 2021; Smith et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to genomic studies.

claim: The genomes of CLE, FLE, and Midichloria underwent massive reduction as observed in other nutritional endosymbionts of arthropods with a specialized diet.
source: As such, the genomes of CLE, FLE, and Midichloria underwent massive reduction as observed in other nutritional endosymbionts of arthropods with a specialized diet (Duron et al., 2018; Gerhart et al., 2018; Gerhart et al., 2016; Gottlieb et al., 2015; Nardi et al., 2021; Sassera et al., 2011; Smith et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to genomic studies.

claim: Hyalomma marginatum is a large tick species that usually feeds on humans and a diversity of mammals and birds in the Mediterranean climatic zone.
source: This large tick species usually feeds on humans and a diversity of mammals and birds in the Mediterranean climatic zone but has recently expanded its range to the north, invading Western Europe (Vial et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Hyalomma marginatum has recently expanded its range to the north, invading Western Europe.
source: This large tick species usually feeds on humans and a diversity of mammals and birds in the Mediterranean climatic zone but has recently expanded its range to the north, invading Western Europe (Vial et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Hyalomma marginatum can transmit Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus.
source: Hyalomma marginatum can transmit Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus, an emerging disease affecting humans in the northern Mediterranean Basin, as well as protozoan parasites and intracellular bacterial pathogens such as Rickettsia aeschlimannii (Vial et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Three microbial metagenomes were sequenced from H. marginatum specimens collected in Spain, Italy, and Israel.
source: We sequenced three microbial metagenomes from H. marginatum specimens collected in Spain (i.e., the Hmar-ES metagenome), Italy (Hmar-IT), and Israel (Hmar-IL).
evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section.

claim: 57,592,510 paired-end reads were obtained from the Hmar-ES metagenome.
source: We obtained 57,592,510 paired-end reads from the Hmar-ES metagenome, 68,515,944 paired-end reads from Hmar-IT, and 10,807,740 paired-end reads from Hmar-IL.
evidence: This is sequencing data reported in the Results section.

claim: One FLE genome with >99% estimated completeness was assembled from each metagenome.
source: We assembled one FLE genome with >99% estimated completeness from each metagenome (FLE-Hmar-ES, FLE-Hmar-IT, and FLE-Hmar-IL; also designated as FLE-Hmar genomes; Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is assembly data reported in the Results section.

claim: One Midichloria genome with >95% estimated completeness was assembled from each metagenome.
source: In parallel, we assembled one genome with >95% estimated completeness from each metagenome for the bacterium Midichloria, and thus obtained three additional complete genomes (Midi-Hmar-ES, Midi-Hmar-IT, and Midi-Hmar-IL; also designated as Midi-Hmar genomes; Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is assembly data reported in the Results section.

claim: R. aeschlimannii was detected in the Hmar-IT and Hmar-IL metagenomes, but not in Hmar-ES.
source: In addition, we detected a third bacterium, the tick-borne pathogen R. aeschlimannii, in the Hmar-IT and Hmar-IL, but not Hmar-ES, metagenomes
evidence: This is detection data reported in the Results section.

claim: The three FLE draft genomes are very similar in size (1.51–1.536 Mb).
source: The assemblies of the three FLE draft genomes (13 contigs for FLE Hmar-IT, 17 for FLE Hmar-ES, and 25 FLE Hmar-IL) were very similar in size (1.51–1.536 Mb)
evidence: This is genomic data reported in the Results section.

claim: The three FLE draft genomes have average G+C content of 31.11–31.23%.
source: The assemblies of the three FLE draft genomes (13 contigs for FLE Hmar-IT, 17 for FLE Hmar-ES, and 25 FLE Hmar-IL) were very similar in size (1.51–1.536 Mb), average G+C content (31.11–31.23%)
evidence: This is genomic data reported in the Results section.

claim: The three FLE draft genomes contain 937–961 predicted protein-coding genes.
source: The assemblies of the three FLE draft genomes (13 contigs for FLE Hmar-IT, 17 for FLE Hmar-ES, and 25 FLE Hmar-IL) were very similar in size (1.51–1.536 Mb), average G+C content (31.11–31.23%), number of predicted protein-coding genes (937–961)
evidence: This is genomic data reported in the Results section.

claim: The three FLE draft genomes contain 789–798 pseudogenes.
source: The assemblies of the three FLE draft genomes (13 contigs for FLE Hmar-IT, 17 for FLE Hmar-ES, and 25 FLE Hmar-IL) were very similar in size (1.51–1.536 Mb), average G+C content (31.11–31.23%), number of predicted protein-coding genes (937–961), and protein-coding sequences with inactivating mutations (pseudogenes, 789–798)
evidence: This is genomic data reported in the Results section.

claim: FLE-Hmar-ES, FLE-Hmar-IT, and FLE-Hmar-IL cluster together in a robust clade within other FLE of ticks.
source: Phylogenomic analysis based on 436 single-copy orthologs (SCOs) Francisella genes showed that FLE-Hmar-ES, FLE-Hmar-IT, and FLE-Hmar-IL cluster together in a robust clade within other FLE of ticks (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenomic analysis and Figure 2A.

claim: The closest relative of the FLE-Hmar clade is the FLE of Hyalomma asiaticum from China.
source: The closest relative of this clade is the FLE of another Hyalomma species, Hyalomma asiaticum from China, while FLEs of other tick genera (Ornithodoros, Argas, and Amblyomma) are more distantly related.
evidence: This is inferred from phylogenomic analysis.

claim: The FLE clade is embedded in the Francisella genus and shares a common origin with pathogenic species, including F. tularensis and F. opportunistica.
source: The FLE clade is embedded in the Francisella genus and shares a common origin with pathogenic species, including the tularemia agent, F. tularensis, and an opportunistic human pathogen, F. opportunistica (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenomic analysis and Figure 2A.

claim: Pseudogenes are highly abundant in the three genomes of FLE of H. marginatum, compared with other FLE genomes.
source: Interestingly, pseudogenes are highly abundant in the three genomes of FLE of H. marginatum, compared with other FLE genomes (Figure 2D)
evidence: This is supported by genomic analysis and Figure 2D.

claim: Most functional categories are impacted by the advanced pseudogenization process in FLE-Hmar genomes.
source: Interestingly, pseudogenes are highly abundant in the three genomes of FLE of H. marginatum, compared with other FLE genomes (Figure 2D), and most functional categories are impacted by this advanced pseudogenization process.
evidence: This is inferred from genomic analysis.

claim: Most genes associated with virulence in pathogenic Francisella species are pseudogenized or completely missing in FLE-Hmar genomes.
source: Most of the genes associated with virulence in pathogenic Francisella species, including the Francisella pathogenicity island (FPI) and secretion system, are pseudogenized or completely missing in FLE-Hmar genomes, consistent with previous observations in other FLEs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by genomic analysis and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: FLE-Hmar genomes contain fewer genes involved in replication, recombination, and repair than any other FLEs analyzed.
source: Furthermore, FLE-Hmar genomes contain fewer genes involved in replication, recombination, and repair than any other FLEs analyzed (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by genomic analysis and Figure 2C.

claim: The nucleotide excision repair system (uvrABCD) in FLE-Hmar genomes is conserved.
source: The nucleotide excision repair system (uvrABCD) in FLE-Hmar genomes is conserved; however, the DNA mismatch repair system (mutSL) is fully pseudogenized.
evidence: This is supported by genomic analysis.

claim: The DNA mismatch repair system (mutSL) is fully pseudogenized in FLE-Hmar genomes.
source: The nucleotide excision repair system (uvrABCD) in FLE-Hmar genomes is conserved; however, the DNA mismatch repair system (mutSL) is fully pseudogenized.
evidence: This is supported by genomic analysis.

claim: The Midichloria genomes reach 1.13–1.16 Mb.
source: The Midichloria genomes, Midi-Hmar-ES, Midi-Hmar-IT, and Midi-Hmar-IL, were assembled in 179, 359, and 123 contigs, respectively, and their genomes reach 1.13–1.16 Mb
evidence: This is genomic data reported in the Results section.

claim: The Midichloria genomes have G+C content of 35.03–35.23%.
source: The Midichloria genomes, Midi-Hmar-ES, Midi-Hmar-IT, and Midi-Hmar-IL, were assembled in 179, 359, and 123 contigs, respectively, and their genomes reach 1.13–1.16 Mb, with consistent G+C content (35.03–35.23%)
evidence: This is genomic data reported in the Results section.

claim: The Midichloria genomes contain 1032–1071 predicted protein-coding genes.
source: The Midichloria genomes, Midi-Hmar-ES, Midi-Hmar-IT, and Midi-Hmar-IL, were assembled in 179, 359, and 123 contigs, respectively, and their genomes reach 1.13–1.16 Mb, with consistent G+C content (35.03–35.23%), number of predicted protein-coding genes (1032–1071)
evidence: This is genomic data reported in the Results section.

claim: The Midichloria genomes contain 190–192 pseudogenes.
source: The Midichloria genomes, Midi-Hmar-ES, Midi-Hmar-IT, and Midi-Hmar-IL, were assembled in 179, 359, and 123 contigs, respectively, and their genomes reach 1.13–1.16 Mb, with consistent G+C content (35.03–35.23%), number of predicted protein-coding genes (1032–1071), pseudogenes (190–192)
evidence: This is genomic data reported in the Results section.

claim: The average coding density of Midichloria genomes (76%) is higher than those of FLEs of H. marginatum (54%).
source: Remarkably, their average coding density (76%) is higher than those of FLEs of H. marginatum (54%), and furthermore, those of other FLE representatives (range from 57% to 69%).
evidence: This is genomic data reported in the Results section.

claim: Midi-Hmar-ES, Midi-Hmar-IT, and Midi-Hmar-IL cluster in a highly supported monophyletic sister group of Candidatus M. mitochondrii strain IricVA.
source: Phylogenomic analysis based on 242 SCOs Rickettsiales genes shows that Midi-Hmar-ES, Midi-Hmar-IT, and Midi-Hmar-IL cluster in a highly supported monophyletic sister group of the single other sequenced Midichloria genome, Candidatus M. mitochondrii strain IricVA (M. mitochondrii hereafter), the intra-mitochondrial endosymbiont of the European sheep tick, Ixodes ricinus.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenomic analysis.

claim: Midichloria genomes delineate a monophyletic clade within the Midichloriaceae family.
source: Altogether, they delineate a monophyletic clade within the Midichloriaceae family (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenomic analysis and Figure 3A.

claim: RAES-Hmar-IT clusters with the tick-associated human pathogen R. aeschlimannii.
source: Phylogenetic analysis based on 324 SCOs genes present in Rickettsia genomes showed that RAES-Hmar-IT clusters with the tick-associated human pathogen R. aeschlimannii (including the strain MC16 previously isolated from H. marginatum) and altogether delineate a robust clade with the Spotted Fever Rickettsia group (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The FLE-Hmar genomes only retain intact pathways for riboflavin and folate.
source: While all previously sequenced FLE genomes contain complete pathways for biotin, riboflavin, and folate, the FLE-Hmar genomes only retain intact pathways for riboflavin and folate (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by genomic analysis and Figure 4A.

claim: The biosynthesis pathway for biotin is non-functional in FLE-Hmar genomes.
source: The biosynthesis pathway for biotin is non-functional, as from six genes of the complete pathway, five (bioA, bioD, bioC, bioF, and bioB) are pseudogenized in the FLE-Hmar genomes (only bioH is not pseudogenized; Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by genomic analysis and Figure 4A.

claim: Five biotin genes (bioA, bioD, bioC, bioF, and bioB) are pseudogenized in the FLE-Hmar genomes.
source: The biosynthesis pathway for biotin is non-functional, as from six genes of the complete pathway, five (bioA, bioD, bioC, bioF, and bioB) are pseudogenized in the FLE-Hmar genomes (only bioH is not pseudogenized; Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by genomic analysis and Figure 4A.

claim: A complete pathway of biotin was consistently recovered in Midichloria genomes.
source: A complete pathway of biotin was consistently recovered in Midichloria genomes (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by genomic analysis and Figure 4A.

claim: Five of the six folate biosynthesis genes (folE, folB, folKP, folC, and folD) were present in Midichloria genomes but the sixth gene, folA, was not.
source: For folate, five of the six biosynthesis genes (folE, folB, folKP, folC, and folD) were present but the sixth gene, folA (encoding for a dihydrofolate reductase), was not.
evidence: This is supported by genomic analysis.

claim: An alternative dihydrofolate reductase gene, folM, was detected in Midichloria genomes.
source: However, we detected an alternative dihydrofolate reductase gene, folM (also known as ydgB), that was shown in other bacteria to provide the same metabolic function as folA (Giladi et al., 2003) suggesting that the folate pathway is functional in Midi-Hmar genomes.
evidence: This is supported by genomic analysis and a citation.

claim: The folate pathway is functional in Midi-Hmar genomes.
source: However, we detected an alternative dihydrofolate reductase gene, folM (also known as ydgB), that was shown in other bacteria to provide the same metabolic function as folA (Giladi et al., 2003) suggesting that the folate pathway is functional in Midi-Hmar genomes.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of folM gene and its known function.

claim: No B vitamin pathway seems complete in the RAES-Hmar genomes.
source: No B vitamin pathway seems complete in the RAES-Hmar genomes.
evidence: This is stated based on genomic analysis.

claim: The FLE-Hmar and Midi-Hmar genomes contain genes involved in heme and iron homeostasis.
source: We thus searched for relevant pathways in the symbiont genomes and found that the FLE-Hmar and Midi-Hmar genomes contain genes involved in heme and iron homeostasis.
evidence: This is supported by genomic analysis.

claim: The heme biosynthetic pathway was consistently detected in FLE-Hmar and Midi-Hmar genomes.
source: The heme biosynthetic pathway was consistently detected, as well as a gene encoding heme oxygenase that catalyzes the degradation of heme and the subsequent release of iron (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by genomic analysis and Figure 4B.

claim: The heme pathway is partially degraded in FLE-Hmar genomes since their hemN gene is pseudogenized.
source: However, the heme pathway is partially degraded in FLE-Hmar genomes since their hemN gene is pseudogenized, a pattern not observed in other FLE genomes, suggesting an early stage of degradation for the heme pathway.
evidence: This is supported by genomic analysis.

claim: The hemN gene is present and not pseudogenized in the Midi-Hmar genomes.
source: This gene is present and not pseudogenized in the Midi-Hmar genomes (Figure 4B), suggesting these symbionts may compensate for the FLE heme pathway.
evidence: This is supported by genomic analysis and Figure 4B.

claim: The B vitamin biosynthesis genes in the FLE-Hmar genomes have all been vertically inherited from a Francisella ancestor.
source: Our analysis shows that the B vitamin biosynthesis genes in the FLE-Hmar genomes have all been vertically inherited from a Francisella ancestor as their B vitamin genes are always more closely related to Francisella orthologous genes than to genes of more distantly related bacteria (examples are shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5A-B).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Folate and riboflavin biosynthesis genes in the Midi-Hmar genomes are of Midichloria origin.
source: Similarly, folate and riboflavin biosynthesis genes in the Midi-Hmar genomes are of Midichloria origin as these genes are more closely related to orthologous genes present in M. mitochondrii and other members of the Midichloriaceae family than to genes of other bacteria (Figure 4—figure supplement 5A-B).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The six biotin genes present in the Midi-Hmar genomes did not originate from the Midichloriaceae family, but from an exogenous origin.
source: By contrast, the six biotin genes present in the Midi-Hmar genomes did not originate from the Midichloriaceae family, but from an exogenous origin.
evidence: This is inferred from phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The biotin synthesis genes bioD, bioC, bioH, bioF, and bioB formed a compact operon in the Midi-Hmar genomes.
source: The biotin synthesis genes bioD, bioC, bioH, bioF, and bioB formed a compact operon in the Midi-Hmar genomes while the bioA gene is more distantly located along the bacterial chromosome (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by genomic analysis and Figure 5.

claim: The biotin synthesis genes were acquired as a whole operon by an ancestor of Midichloria from an unrelated intracellular bacterium.
source: Phylogenetic analyses of the six biotin synthesis genes consistently exhibited similar evolutionary patterns (Figure 5). These patterns suggest that the biotin synthesis genes were acquired as a whole operon by an ancestor of Midichloria from an unrelated intracellular bacterium.
evidence: This is inferred from phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: FLE and Midichloria are both abundant in H. marginatum ovaries.
source: Real-time qPCR assays on 10 field H. marginatum adult females indicated that FLE and Midichloria are both abundant in tick ovaries, with FLE and Midichloria detected in 10 and 9 ovarian samples, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data.

claim: FLE were consistently most abundant with densities 5.8–21.4× higher than Midichloria densities.
source: FLE were consistently most abundant with densities 5.8–21.4× higher than Midichloria densities (paired t-test, p=0.013; one outlier was removed from analysis, n=8).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data and statistical analysis.

claim: The FLE and Midichloria densities covaried positively in individual ticks.
source: The FLE and Midichloria densities covaried positively in individual ticks (χ2=23.937, p=0.003; Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and Figure 6B.

claim: Out of 10 Hyalomma species with sufficient published data, all were found infected by FLE, and 9 by Midichloria.
source: Out of 10 Hyalomma species with sufficient published data, all were found infected by FLE, and 9 by Midichloria (Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: This is based on a bibliographic survey.

claim: Co-infection by FLE and Midichloria is widespread across all Hyalomma lineages.
source: Mapping of FLE and Midichloria onto the Hyalomma phylogenetic tree showed that co-infection by FLE and Midichloria is widespread across all Hyalomma lineages (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is inferred from phylogenetic mapping shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: FLE and Midichloria co-infection was not detected in H. asiaticum.
source: However, FLE and Midichloria co-infection was not detected in one species, H. asiaticum, nested within the Hyalomma phylogeny among co-infected species.
evidence: This is based on bibliographic survey and phylogenetic analysis.

claim: H. marginatum harbors a microbiome functionally analogous to those observed in other tick species, dominated by intracellular bacterial symbionts producing biotin, riboflavin, and folate.
source: This tick harbors a microbiome functionally analogous to those observed in other tick species, dominated by intracellular bacterial symbionts producing the core set of B vitamins (biotin, riboflavin, and folate) essential for tick growth and survival.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the study's findings.

claim: In other tick species, production of all three core B vitamins is performed by a single nutritional symbiont.
source: However, while in other tick species, as in other obligate blood feeders, production of all three core B vitamins is performed by a single nutritional symbiont (Binetruy et al., 2020; Duron et al., 2017; Duron and Gottlieb, 2020)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: H. marginatum harbors two bacterial partners whose core B vitamins biosynthetic capacities depend on a combination of genes, with indigenous and exogenous phylogenetic origins.
source: H. marginatum harbors two bacterial partners whose core B vitamins biosynthetic capacities depend on a combination of genes, with indigenous and exogenous phylogenetic origins.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the study's findings.

claim: Genetically similar FLE and Midichloria are present in H. marginatum populations from geographically distant regions.
source: This multi-partner nutritional symbiosis is stably maintained at least at the tick species level, as supported by our founding of genetically similar FLE and Midichloria present in H. marginatum populations from geographically distant regions.
evidence: This is inferred from the genomic data from three geographic locations.

claim: Genome reduction is a conserved trait in all FLEs.
source: Genome reduction is a conserved trait in all FLEs, but this process has extended in the FLE of H. marginatum, with an additional loss of genes in most COG functional categories.
evidence: This is inferred from comparative genomic analysis.

claim: The pseudogenization of the mismatch repair system (mutSL) could have triggered the extended genome reduction in FLE of H. marginatum.
source: This process could have been triggered by the pseudogenization of the mismatch repair system (mutSL), leaving the FLE of H. marginatum with only one DNA repair system, nucleotide excision repair (uvrABCD).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on genomic data.

claim: Absence of the mutSL system, coupled with strict clonality and a small population size during transovarial transmission, have probably led the FLE-Hmar genomes to accumulate deleterious mutations.
source: Absence of the mutSL system, coupled with strict clonality and a small population size during transovarial transmission, have probably led the FLE- Hmar genomes to accumulate deleterious mutations, that resulted in maladaptation, and ultimately limited their beneficial contributions to ticks.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on genomic data and evolutionary theory.

claim: Co-infection with Midichloria prevents the breakdown and collapse of nutritional symbiosis in H. marginatum.
source: In the context of FLE genome degradation, co-infection with Midichloria prevents the breakdown and collapse of nutritional symbiosis in H. marginatum; that is, the Midichloria genome contains an intact biotin biosynthesis operon, and thus compensates for genome decay of FLE.
evidence: This is inferred from the complementary genomic capabilities of the two symbionts.

claim: Midichloria has only partial pathways for riboflavin and folate and hence cannot meet the nutritional needs of H. marginatum for these B vitamins.
source: Inversely, Midichloria has only partial pathways for riboflavin and folate and hence cannot meet the nutritional needs of H. marginatum for these B vitamins.
evidence: This is inferred from genomic analysis.

claim: The co-infection of FLE with Midichloria forms a cooperative system essential for the nutritional symbiosis in H. marginatum.
source: Consequently, the co-infection of FLE with Midichloria forms a cooperative system essential for the nutritional symbiosis in H. marginatum.
evidence: This is inferred from the complementary genomic capabilities of the two symbionts.

claim: Complete biosynthetic heme gene pathways exist in most animals, but not in ticks that need an exogenous source of heme.
source: Complete biosynthetic heme gene pathways exist in most animals, but not in ticks that need an exogenous source of heme (Gulia-Nuss, 2016; Jia et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Vertebrate blood is usually considered to be the unique source of heme for ticks.
source: Vertebrate blood is usually considered to be their unique source for this essential cofactor (Perner et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The presence of heme genes in FLE and Midichloria genomes may indicate symbiont provisioning of heme in H. marginatum.
source: however ticks spend most of their life off host, and thus the presence of heme genes in FLE and Midichloria genomes may also indicate symbiont provisioning of heme in H. marginatum.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on genomic data and tick biology.

claim: The co-localization of FLE and Midichloria in tick ovaries suggests that vertical transmission has led to their stable co-inheritance through tick generations.
source: The co-localization of FLE and Midichloria in tick ovaries suggests that vertical transmission has led to their stable co-inheritance through tick generations, linking their evolutionary fate, as observed in other symbiotic systems of arthropods (McCutcheon et al., 2019; Vautrin and Vavre, 2009).
evidence: This is inferred from localization data and supported by citations.

claim: The covariance of FLE and Midichloria densities in ticks is positive, suggesting that these two symbionts are not in direct competition but rather cooperative.
source: Furthermore, the covariance of FLE and Midichloria densities in ticks is positive, suggesting that these two symbionts are not in direct competition but rather cooperative.
evidence: This is inferred from statistical analysis of density data.

claim: FLE is about 100-times more abundant than Midichloria.
source: However, FLE is about 100-times more abundant than Midichloria, which can be suggestive of competition.
evidence: This is inferred from the density data.

claim: FLE and Midichloria depend on each other since their host tick would not survive without their combined production of B vitamins.
source: Regardless of the issue of this interaction, FLE and Midichloria depend on each other since their host tick would not survive without their combined production of B vitamins.
evidence: This is inferred from the complementary genomic capabilities and known importance of B vitamins.

claim: The nutritional association of FLE with Hyalomma species has persisted for millions of years.
source: While the nutritional association of FLE with Hyalomma species has persisted for millions of years (Azagi et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The nutritional role of Midichloria seems more recent in the Hyalomma genus.
source: While the nutritional association of FLE with Hyalomma species has persisted for millions of years (Azagi et al., 2017), the nutritional role of Midichloria seems more recent in this tick genus.
evidence: This is inferred from the distribution pattern across Hyalomma species.

claim: In most Hyalomma species, Midichloria is present at much lower frequencies than would be expected for an obligate nutritional mutualist.
source: Co-infection with Midichloria was reported in at least nine Hyalomma species (Supplementary file 1d), but in most species, such as H. excavatum and H. impeltatum (Azagi et al., 2017; Selmi et al., 2019), Midichloria is present at much lower frequencies than would be expected for an obligate nutritional mutualist, suggesting that it is instead a facultative (i.e., not essential) association.
evidence: This is inferred from prevalence data and supported by citations.

claim: H. asiaticum harbors an FLE with intact biotin, folate, and riboflavin synthesis pathways.
source: Interestingly, the Hyalomma species apparently devoid of Midichloria, H. asiaticum, harbors an FLE with intact biotin, folate, and riboflavin synthesis pathways (Buysse and Duron, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The decay of the FLE genome in H. marginatum may have been accelerated by the presence of Midichloria and the redundancy of biotin biosynthesis.

claim: The streamlined biotin operon has experienced transfers between distantly related endosymbionts inhabiting arthropod cells including Wolbachia, Rickettsia, Cardinium, and Legionella.

source: While past investigations showed that this evolutionary convergence consists in severe degeneration of symbiont genomes accompanied by preservation of biotin, folate, and riboflavin biosynthesis pathways (Buysse and Duron, 2021; Duron and Gottlieb, 2020), nutritional endosymbiosis in H. marginatum is influenced by a more complex web of interactions resulting in a dynamic mosaic of symbiont combinations and offering novel evolutionary possibilities.
